To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the AM fungal hyphal uptake of nitrogen from the soil is mediated by the high-affinity ammonium transporters (AMT) and the low-affinity ammonium transporter (LAT) proteins.

1. The nitrogen uptake, assimilations and translocation in AM symbiosis are complex, which involve the interplay of plant and fungal transporters and enzymes; 2. The N status and interplays of C and P in plants can regulate the formation and functioning of the AM symbiosis.

1) AM fungi can acquire N from the soil via the AM symbiosis and can also acquire N from the plant via the AM symbiotic interfaces, 2) AM fungi can transport N to the plant and can also transport N from the plant to the soil, 3) AM fungi can assimilate N from ammonium or nitrate to amino acids, and can transport amino acids to the host plant via the AM interfaces, 4) AM plants can assimilate N in the roots
In summary, our research is concerned with

the transport properties and regulatory roles that nitrogen plays in AM symbiosis, which may provide a basis for further studies on the molecular mechanisms underlying the AM symbiosis and the regulation of nutrient uptake and allocation.
the transport and regulation of nitrogen in the AM symbiotic interface, and its impact on plant growth, nutrient uptake, and symbiosis development.
the transport of nitrogen and the role of nitrogen in AM symbiosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
N is a key factor regulating the AM symbiosis.
N is a key regulator for AM symbiosis, but its regulatory role is still largely unclear and needs to be elucidated in the future.

the AM symbiosis is an efficient strategy for plants to acquire N under N-limiting soil conditions, and the symbiotic N uptake and assimilation is a complex process involving the coordinated regulation of the plant-fungus interaction, the host N status, and the interplay with C metabolism and P uptake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the AM symbiosis is a complex system, in which the plant and fungal partners interact to optimize the uptake of mineral nutrients, especially N, and to balance the C and N metabolism.

AM fungi are important in the N nutrition of plants and the AM symbiosis is a dynamic and complex process in which the C and N status of plants and the C and P status of the AM fungal partner play important roles in the establishment and functioning of AM symbiosis.
N availability and N status in AM plants can affect the development of AM symbiosis and the transport and allocation of C and P in AM plants.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the AM symbiosis is a dynamic process that can be influenced by the availability and the ratio of nutrients in the soil, and the AM fungal partners may have a greater impact on the N status of their hosts than previously appreciated.
AM fungi can enhance the N uptake by the host plant and the AM symbiosis can also regulate the N metabolism in the host plants.
AM fungi and plants are able to regulate N uptake and assimilation to optimize the N use efficiency and to balance the C and P demands in response to N availability.
